Celibacy
SEL-uh-buh-see
doctrinal phrase
From Latin caelibatus, the unmarried state; the condition of remaining unmarried, especially for the sake of undistracted service to God.

Biblical Definition

Celibacy is the state of remaining unmarried, which Scripture honors as a lawful and, for some, a gifted calling for the sake of undistracted service to God—while firmly rejecting the imposition of compulsory celibacy as a requirement for office or a higher class of holiness. The Lord Jesus spoke of those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake, and bade him receive it who is able. The apostle Paul, himself unmarried, commended the single state for its freedom from the cares that attend marriage, that the unmarried might care for the things of the Lord without distraction and attend upon Him without hindrance; yet he expressly named singleness a gift not given to all, taught that it is better to marry than to burn, and honored marriage as honorable in all. Celibacy in Scripture is therefore neither commanded nor exalted above marriage, but left free: a good calling for those gifted and willing, undertaken for service, not as a meritorious work. The dictionary holds this biblical balance against the Roman corruption that forbids marriage to its priests and elevates the celibate religious life as a counsel of perfection. Paul named the forbidding of marriage among the doctrines of devils that mark a falling away from the faith; what God has left free, the church may not bind. The dictionary commends celibacy where it is a genuine gift for the kingdom’s service, honors the marriage God ordained for the rest, and rejects every system that makes the single state a law, a merit, or a higher holiness.

Webster 1828 Definition

The unmarried state, honored in Scripture as a lawful and gifted calling for undistracted service to God—but never commanded, never meritorious, and not to be imposed as compulsory.

CELIBACY, the state of remaining unmarried.

Honored for some as a gifted calling for undistracted service to God.

Christ’s “eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake”; Paul commends the single state.

A gift not given to all; “it is better to marry than to burn.”

Neither commanded nor exalted above marriage; the forbidding of marriage is condemned.

Key Scripture

1Co 7:7 — "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that."

1Co 7:32 — "But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord:"

Mat 19:12 — "For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it."

1Ti 4:3 — "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth."

Modern Corruption

Celibacy is corrupted into a compulsory law for clergy and a higher class of holiness, against the freedom Scripture leaves.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption is the Roman imposition of compulsory celibacy upon its priests and the elevation of the celibate religious life as a counsel of perfection—a higher holiness than the married estate. Scripture leaves the single state free, a gift for some and a calling for service, never a law or a merit. Paul names the forbidding of marriage among the “doctrines of devils” that mark a departure from the faith, and the qualifications for elder assume a married man, “the husband of one wife.” What God has left free, the church may not bind, and the mandatory celibacy of the clergy has borne bitter fruit through the centuries.

The dictionary holds the biblical balance. Celibacy is honorable where it is a genuine gift, undertaken willingly for undistracted devotion to the Lord, and the church should esteem the single believer who serves Christ without the cares of marriage. But it is not superior to marriage, which God ordained at creation and pronounced good; it is not meritorious, earning no special favor; and it is not to be imposed. Against both the Roman exaltation of compulsory celibacy and any modern disdain for the single life, the dictionary keeps the apostolic freedom: marriage is honorable in all, singleness is a good gift for some, and each is to serve God in the calling he is given.

Hebrew Roots

The word names the unmarried state, honored as a gift for service but never commanded, meritorious, or imposed.

expand to see more

Latin caelibatus — the unmarried state, from caelebs, unmarried.

Christ’s “eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake” (Matthew 19:12).

Greek charisma — gift; singleness a “proper gift of God” for some.

Paul’s counsel: the unmarried “careth for the things... of the Lord.”

“Forbidding to marry” named among the “doctrines of devils.”

Usage

"Celibacy is honored as a gifted calling for undistracted service to the Lord."

"Paul’s teaching is cited that it is a gift not given to all and not above marriage."

"It is set against the Roman imposition of compulsory clerical celibacy."
